passage: Yamini, since you're flat-hunting, sit and listen. I am Keerthana, and at twenty-one I found a lovely room in Hyderabad. The landlord's first message asked, "Surname? Vegetarian or non-veg? Which state?" I answered, and an hour later the room was "taken". A friend saw the same room advertised again the next day. I felt small first, then furious. Then I made myself act. I saved every message with its date, told two friends who had been turned away by the same man, and together we took it to a tenants' group in the city, where a volunteer explained that it was discrimination and how we could make a formal complaint. Nobody promised the man would change. But we found another room within the week, and I stopped thinking the fault was in my surname.

passage:
Dear Joseph,
You said to write down everything, so here it is.
I found a room near the college gate, the rent I could afford, and the owner was friendly on the phone. When I arrived he asked my full name. Then he asked, "What do your people eat? Meat?" Then, "Where is your native place, exactly?" Then he said the room was "just taken."
Twenty minutes later my classmate from Delhi called the same number and was told it was free.
I'm writing it all down, like you said: date, time, the questions, his exact words, my classmate's call. I'm not going to argue with him again. That's discrimination, even if he's polite about it.
Our college's student welfare office has a legal-aid volunteer on Wednesdays. Will you come with me? I'd feel steadier with you there.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did the owner say about the room?
qa.a: He said the room was "just taken."

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about going to the welfare office?
qa.a: Bhupen feels shaken and would feel steadier with Joseph there, showing some anxiety as well as determination.

qa.q: Which steps Bhupen is taking are mature ones?
qa.a: Bhupen names it as discrimination, writes down the date, questions and exact words, and plans to see the legal-aid volunteer with an ally instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's classmate from Delhi feel about what happened?
qa.a: The classmate might feel angry and uncomfortable to learn the same room was offered to them and refused to Bhupen.

Divyansh, thanks for having me on. People ask about the job I didn't get, so here it is.
Final round, three people on the panel. Technical questions went well. Then one of them looked at my CV and said, "Aparna... and your surname is? What community is that?" Another asked, "Your family is vegetarian?" None of it had anything to do with the role.
I remember my face going hot and my mind going blank. I answered. I didn't get the job.
Afterwards I did three things. I wrote down every question and the time. I spoke to my college placement cell, and two other students said the same panel had asked them the same things. And we went together to a legal-aid clinic to understand what we could do.
The company changed its panel guidelines after our complaint. I still didn't get that job. But Aparna made some noise, and that counts.

qa.q: What did one panel member ask about Aparna's family?
qa.a: Another asked, "Your family is vegetarian?"

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling during those questions?
qa.a: Aparna felt humiliated and shocked, with a mind gone blank at questions that had nothing to do with the role.

qa.q: What did Aparna do afterwards that was wise?
qa.a: Aparna wrote down every question, found other students who had been asked the same things, and went with them to a legal-aid clinic.

qa.q: How might the two other students have felt when Aparna spoke up?
qa.a: They were probably relieved that someone named the problem, and less alone in their own experience.

passage:
Day one. Jahnavi, twenty, from Manipur, called about a flat near her new internship in Gurugram. The broker's voice changed when he heard her name. "Owner prefers north Indians. Family types," he said, and hung up.
Day three. She went to see another flat with her office friend Tarun. The owner asked Jahnavi, "Do you cook smelly food? Your people eat dogs?" Tarun stiffened. Jahnavi said calmly, "I'm here for the flat, sir." They left. On the stairs, her hands were trembling. Tarun said, "That's discrimination. Let's write it all down."
Day six. At her office's HR desk, Jahnavi and Tarun showed a notebook: dates, names, the broker's number, the exact questions. HR connected her with a legal-aid group and a list of owners who had signed a fair-housing pledge. Jahnavi moved into one of those flats the next week.

qa.q: Where is Jahnavi's new internship?
qa.a: Her new internship is in Gurugram.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling on the stairs?
qa.a: She felt shaken and humiliated, her hands trembling after staying calm in front of the owner.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi and Tarun respond wisely?
qa.a: They named it as discrimination, wrote down dates, names and questions, and took the notes to HR, which connected her with legal aid and fair owners.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt watching the owner's questions?
qa.a: Tarun stiffened, which suggests he felt angry and embarrassed on Jahnavi's behalf, and it pushed him to support her.

passage: Mehak, you asked why I keep every paper in that tin box. Let your Jagdish Chacha tell you. I was twenty, new in Pune, with a job letter in my pocket. The landlord was polite on the phone. At the door he asked my full surname, then whether we ate meat, then which district my people came from. That evening the room was "already given". Next day my friend Suresh phoned the same man and was offered it at once. I was angry enough to shout. Instead I wrote down every question with the date and time, and I asked Suresh to write down what he heard. A lawyer at the workers' union read my notes and sent a letter. I never lived there, beta. But the next tenant was asked no such questions.

qa.a: He was angry enough to shout, and probably hurt, sensing he had been judged by surname and food rather than by his job letter.

qa.a: Notes with dates, times and a second witness turned a suspicion into evidence that the union lawyer could act on.
